corrected_value.title: Interpersonal movement synchrony facilitates pro-social behavior in childrens peer-play.

decisions.quote:
The primary aim of the current study is to extend previous research by examining if

interpersonal synchrony has real world significance in improving children’s helping and empathy

behaviors. This will be done by replicating established tasks conducted by Tunçgenç & Cohen

(2016b), with helping and empathy measurements completed before and after the

synchronization task.
decisions.reason: Kirschner & Tomasello (2010) tested joint music making (marching and singing) and only supplied the fish-feeding helping task/measure used in Tunçgenç & Cohen (2016b) and in the present study. Per codebook rules excluding papers that only supply a task/measure and selecting the closest study in a replication chain, the actual target re-tested here is Tunçgenç & Cohen (2016b) (10.1111/desc.12505, blind target_index 0), whose non-musical clapping/tapping synchrony paradigm, social bonding measures (eye contact and smiles), and prosocial helping findings this thesis directly replicates and compares against.

decisions.quote:
Despite findings from Tunçgenç & Cohen (2016b), the results from the current study

reveal that interpersonal synchrony does not lead to increased instrumental helping and social

bonding behaviors in three- to five-year-old children when paired with an adult partner.
decisions.reason: With the dependent original identity resolved to Tunçgenç & Cohen (2016b) (blind target_index 0), the author explicitly concludes in the Abstract and Discussion that the replication failed: contrary to Tunçgenç & Cohen (2016b), interpersonal movement synchrony did not lead to higher instrumental helping, empathy, or social bonding behaviors (eye contact and individual/mutual smiles) compared with asynchrony. Secondary peer-pair extension issues in Experiment 2 and general limitations do not alter the author's clear overall negative verdict.
